title: Bridging integrated-light and resolved-star studies of Local Group dwarf spheroidals. A novel use of deep imaging based on amateur telescopes
comment: 17 pages, 17 figures. Accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics on August 30, 2026
summary: Low-mass galaxies beyond the Local Group can only be studied through their integrated light, yet it remains unclear whether structural parameters inferred from integrated light are directly comparable to those obtained from resolved-star studies. Using new deep imaging obtained with small-aperture amateur telescopes, we analyse the classical dwarf spheroidals Leo II, Sculptor, and Fornax, whose stellar distributions have been extensively characterised through resolved-star studies. We find that the radial light distributions and effective radii inferred from integrated light are in excellent agreement with those derived from resolved stars, showing that resolved-star and integrated-light analyses can be placed within a common observational framework applicable across a broad range of distances. The two approaches are highly complementary: resolved-star analyses trace galaxies to very large radii but are limited by stellar crowding in their central regions, whereas integrated-light observations are insensitive to crowding and allow the inner stellar distribution to be traced to substantially smaller radii. The integrated-light analysis extends the structural analysis to radii up to an order of magnitude smaller than previous star-counting studies while significantly reducing the scatter in the measured profiles.

AI.tldr: Using deep imaging from small-aperture amateur telescopes, integrated-light structural parameters (radial light distributions and effective radii) of three classical dwarf spheroidal galaxies (Leo II, Sculptor, Fornax) agree excellently with resolved-star measurements, demonstrating the two observational approaches are complementary and comparable across a wide range of distances.
AI.motivation: For low-mass galaxies beyond the Local Group, only integrated-light observations are possible, yet it is unclear whether structural parameters derived from integrated light are directly comparable to those from resolved-star studies, which are available only for nearby systems.
AI.method: Deep imaging with small-aperture amateur telescopes was used to analyse integrated light from classical dwarf spheroidal galaxies Leo II, Sculptor, and Fornax—systems whose stellar distributions are well characterised by resolved-star studies—enabling a direct comparison of the two methods.
AI.result: Integrated-light radial profiles and effective radii agree excellently with resolved-star results, and the integrated-light approach extends structural analysis to radii up to an order of magnitude smaller than star-counting studies while significantly reducing scatter in the measured profiles.
AI.conclusion: Resolved-star and integrated-light analyses can be placed within a common observational framework applicable across a broad range of distances and are highly complementary: resolved-star studies probe to large radii but suffer from central crowding, whereas integrated-light observations are crowding-insensitive and trace the inner stellar distribution to substantially smaller radii.

title: Classical Cepheids in the Nuclear Stellar Disk: membership via dynamical analysis
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A. 10 pages and 14 figures in the main text, 4 pages and 8 figures in the appendix
summary: (abridged) Four classical Cepheids have been associated to the Nuclear Stellar Disk (NSD), suggesting a burst of star formation 20 Myrs ago. In this work, we analyse all available data for these four Cepheids in order to gauge if they are bona fide members of the NSD or interlopers in the region. This allows to confirm or rule out the star formation burst hypothesised in the literature. Our dynamical analysis is based on an updated MWpotential that includes all components of the inner Galaxy. We conduct a thorough study of possible systematics, taking into account both observational errors and model dependencies. Our results suggest that only one Cepheid likely belongs to the NSD, while the orbits of other two extend well beyond it. Accounting for observational uncertainties, only 23-28 percent of the realisations sourced from the error distributions for the latter two are compatible with the NSD. For the fourth there are no proper motion measurements available and the light curve analysis puts into question its classification as a classical Cepheid. Through a comprehensive dynamical analysis of available data on the Cepheids attributed to the NSD, we gauged their membership to this structure. Out of the three Cepheids analysed in unprecedented depth, GCC-a is likely a member of the NSD while both GCC-b and GCC-c do not seem dynamically linked to it. Factoring in the observational uncertainties, a non-negligible percentage of the realisations for GCC-b and GCC-c are still compatible with the NSD, thus membership cannot be completely excluded for either with current data. The robust association of only one Cepheid casts doubt on the occurrence of a star formation episode in the NSD, about 20 Myrs ago.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether four classical Cepheids previously associated with the Nuclear Stellar Disk (NSD) of the Milky Way are genuine members or interlopers, to test the hypothesized 20 Myr old star formation burst. Using an updated Milky Way potential and accounting for observational and model uncertainties, the authors find that only one Cepheid (GCC-a) is likely a genuine NSD member, while two others (GCC-b and GCC-c) have orbits extending beyond the NSD, and a fourth lacks proper motion data and is questionable as a classical Cepheid. This casts doubt on the claimed recent star formation episode in the NSD.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to verify whether four classical Cepheids attributed to the Nuclear Stellar Disk (NSD) of the Milky Way are genuine members or interlopers, in order to confirm or rule out the hypothesized 20 Myr old star formation burst within the NSD that previous literature suggested based on these Cepheids.
AI.method: The authors perform a dynamical analysis of the four Cepheids using an updated Milky Way gravitational potential that includes all inner Galaxy components. They integrate orbits and assess each star's membership to the NSD. A thorough treatment of systematics is conducted, incorporating both observational errors and model dependencies, and they sample from error distributions to quantify the fraction of orbit realizations compatible with NSD membership. Light curve analysis is also used to validate the Cepheid classification.
AI.result: Only one of the Cepheids (GCC-a) is likely a genuine member of the NSD. The orbits of two others (GCC-b and GCC-c) extend well beyond the NSD, with only 23-28% of error-distribution realizations being compatible with NSD membership. The fourth Cepheid has no proper motion data and its classification as a classical Cepheid is questioned by light curve analysis.
AI.conclusion: The robust association of only a single Cepheid with the NSD casts doubt on the occurrence of a recent (about 20 Myr ago) star formation episode within the Nuclear Stellar Disk. However, since a non-negligible fraction of orbital realizations for GCC-b and GCC-c remain NSD-compatible given current observational uncertainties, their membership cannot be completely ruled out with present data.

title: Evolution of bar-induced dark gaps in galaxy discs: evidence of strong bar-driven effects already at $z > 2$
comment: 12 pages, 13 figures (including appendices), accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The properties of stellar bars play a crucial role in determining the bar-driven secular evolution in disc galaxies. However, a systematic observational study of the evolution of several bar properties (such as strength and length) across cosmic time is largely missing. In this paper, using a sample of $625$ barred galaxies, taken from SDSS, HST COSMOS, and JWST CEERS surveys, we systematically investigate the evolution of bar properties over redshifts ($0.02 \lesssim z < 3$) by making a novel usage of dark gap (preferential light deficit along the bar minor axis) properties as a proxy for bar properties. We show that the dark gap strength ($Δμ_{\rm max}$) exhibits a weak evolution, increasing from higher redshifts ($z \sim 2.5$) and slightly declining towards lower redshifts ($z < 0.05$). Conversely, the extent of dark gaps ($R_{\rm DG}, R_{\rm dark}$; normalised by bar length) decreases moderately from $z \geq 1.4$ and remains constant thereafter. Our results suggest that bar formation and the initial rapid growth phase occur before $z \sim 3$, followed by mild growth towards lower redshifts. We also find $R_{\rm dark}$ to be a better proxy (as compared to $R_{\rm DG}$) for estimating bar length, supporting earlier theoretical studies. Furthermore, the $Δμ_{\rm max}$ shows a weak but statistically significant correlation with bar-to-total light ratio (Bar/T) and bar ellipticity ($ε_{\rm bar}$). Studies of the redshift evolution of bar properties over such an extensive redshift range as done here are instrumental in constraining the bar-driven evolution at early cosmic times.

AI.tldr: Using 625 barred galaxies from SDSS, HST COSMOS, and JWST CEERS, this paper systematically studies the evolution of bar properties across redshifts 0.02 ≤ z < 3 by employing dark gap properties as a proxy. Dark gap strength shows weak evolution (peak near low z, slight decline below z<0.05), while dark gap extent decreases moderately from z≥1.4 and stays constant. Results suggest bars form and grow rapidly before z~3 with mild growth afterward.
AI.motivation: Stellar bars drive secular evolution in disc galaxies, yet a systematic observational study of how multiple bar properties (strength, length, etc.) evolve across cosmic time is largely missing.
AI.method: Analysis of 625 barred galaxies from three surveys (SDSS, HST COSMOS, JWST CEERS) spanning z~0.02 to z<3, using dark gap properties (light deficits along the bar minor axis) as a novel proxy to trace bar properties. Correlations between dark gap strength and bar-to-total light ratio and bar ellipticity are examined.
AI.result: Dark gap strength (Δμ_max) evolves weakly: increases from high z (~2.5) into low redshifts, declining slightly below z<0.05. Dark gap extents (R_DG, R_dark) normalized by bar length decrease moderately from z≥1.4 then remain constant. R_dark is a better proxy for bar length than R_DG. Δμ_max shows weak but statistically significant correlation with Bar/T and bar ellipticity.
AI.conclusion: Bar formation and initial rapid growth occurred before z~3, followed by mild growth toward lower redshifts. Dark gap properties, particularly R_dark, provide effective proxies for studying bar evolution, enabling constraints on bar-driven secular evolution at early cosmic times.

title: Same galaxy, different CGM: how the metal loading of galactic winds regulates the baryon cycle in Milky Way-mass galaxies
comment: 17 pages, 12 figures; submitted to MNRAS; comments are welcome
summary: The circumgalactic medium (CGM) is both the reservoir of gas that fuels star formation and galaxy growth, and the repository for the mass, energy, and metals expelled through stellar evolution and feedback. We present a controlled experiment using a suite of five cosmological magnetohydrodynamical simulations of a Milky Way-mass halo from the Auriga suite, where we vary the metal content and energy loading of galactic winds driven by stellar feedback. We chose these parameters in combination such that all five runs obtain very similar (within $\approx$10\%) $z=0$ stellar masses and morphologies and thus produce similar amounts of metals throughout their lifetimes. Our simulations differ substantially in where these metals end up, spatially within the halo and across the different baryonic components (stars, gas disc, CGM, and the intergalactic medium). The metal content affects the cooling efficiency of the halo gas, regulating the CGM cool gas fraction and the accretion rates onto the galaxy. Between our two extreme models, we report an order of magnitude difference in the median gas metallicity at vertical heights $|z| \gtrsim 30$ kpc above the disc plane. Current constraints on the metallicity of the Milky Way halo gas from absorption-line measurements of intermediate- and high-velocity clouds at $|z| \lesssim 15$ kpc are broadly consistent with our simulations, though a direct comparison is limited by differences in the adopted methods. Our findings show that galaxies with nearly identical stellar content and morphology can differ substantially in their CGM, which offers a promising avenue for constraining feedback physics within galaxy formation models.

AI.tldr: Using five Auriga cosmological magnetohydrodynamical simulations of a Milky Way-mass halo with varying wind metal content and energy loading (tuned to yield nearly identical stellar masses and morphologies), the study shows that metals can end up in very different baryonic reservoirs (stars, gas disc, CGM, IGM) depending on feedback parameters. This causes up to an order-of-magnitude difference in median gas metallicity at high vertical heights, and their CGM predictions are broadly consistent with Milky Way absorption-line measurements.
AI.motivation: The CGM is the key interface between gas accretion and feedback-driven outflows, yet it is poorly constrained. The authors aim to test how much the CGM varies between galaxies that are otherwise indistinguishable in stellar content and morphology, which could offer observational leverage on feedback physics.
AI.method: A controlled experiment with five cosmological magnetohydrodynamical simulations of a Milky Way-mass halo from the Auriga suite. Wind metal content and energy loading are varied in combination to keep z=0 stellar masses and morphologies consistent (~10%). Metal distribution is tracked spatially across baryonic components (stars, gas disc, CGM, IGM), and predictions are compared to absorption-line metallicity constraints on the Milky Way's halo gas.
AI.result: The simulations produce similar stellar content but differ substantially in where metals reside—spatially and across baryonic components. Metal-enriched gas changes halo cooling efficiency, regulating CGM cool gas fraction and galactic accretion rates. An order-of-magnitude difference in median gas metallicity appears at |z| ≳ 30 kpc between extreme models. Current Milky Way halo gas metallicity constraints from intermediate- and high-velocity clouds at |z| ≲ 15 kpc are broadly consistent, though direct comparison is limited by methodological differences.
AI.conclusion: Galaxies with nearly identical stellar content and morphology can differ dramatically in their CGM properties. This diversity provides a promising observational avenue for constraining feedback physics within galaxy formation models.

title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Emulators of Stellar Evolution for Precision Asteroseismology
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures, accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Fast and accurate stellar evolution emulators---surrogate models that approximate expensive simulation outputs with machine learning (ML)---are powerful tools for modern stellar characterization, hierarchical inference, and population synthesis. We analyze the grid density required for reliable emulation by training ML algorithms on main-sequence models with masses M=[0.7,1.2] solar masses. This range is challenging to emulate due to rapidly varying evolutionary behavior caused by the radiative-to-convective core transition, as well as the requirement to match the part-per-thousand seismic precision that has been delivered for such stars from the NASA Kepler mission. Generating grids from analytical models, as well as MESA, YREC, MIST, and ASTEC, we compare linear interpolation, k-nearest neighbors, random forests, and neural networks (NNs) in interpolating the stellar observables: T_eff, L, Delta nu, and nu_max. While NNs outperform other methods, sparse grids induce localized failures in the core-transition region, resulting in unstable derivatives, ensemble disagreement, and fragmented posterior distributions during inference. Performance gains from denser grids are non-uniform, suggesting that adaptive grid generation should be favored over uniform refinement. Finally, we show that NN ensembles allow for localized uncertainty propagation, more accurately reflecting emulator reliability across parameter space than global uncertainty estimates. As we consider only the two-dimensional case of varying only stellar mass and age along the main sequence, these results represent a lower bound on the challenge in emulating stellar evolution simulations for precision asteroseismology.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the grid density required for reliable emulation of stellar evolution simulations using machine learning surrogates, focusing on main-sequence models with masses 0.7-1.2 solar masses. It compares multiple ML methods (linear interpolation, k-NN, random forests, neural networks) across various stellar evolution codes and finds that neural networks perform best, but sparse grids cause localized failures near the radiative-to-convective core transition. The authors recommend adaptive grid generation over uniform refinement and demonstrate that NN ensembles provide localized uncertainty propagation.
AI.motivation: To determine the grid density requirements and optimal ML emulation strategies for stellar evolution models, particularly in the challenging mass range where core transition behavior causes rapid evolutionary changes and where seismic precision demands are stringent.
AI.method: Training multiple ML algorithms (linear interpolation, k-nearest neighbors, random forests, and neural networks) on main-sequence stellar evolution models with masses M=[0.7,1.2] solar masses. Grids were generated from analytical models and four stellar evolution codes (MESA, YREC, MIST, ASTEC), with emulation tested on observables including T_eff, L, Delta nu, and nu_max.
AI.result: Neural networks outperform other interpolation methods. However, sparse grids cause localized failures in the core-transition region leading to unstable derivatives, ensemble disagreement, and fragmented posterior distributions. Denser grids provide non-uniform performance gains, and NN ensembles enable localized (rather than global) uncertainty propagation that better reflects emulator reliability.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive grid generation should be preferred over uniform refinement for stellar evolution emulation. NN ensembles offer superior localized uncertainty characterization. Since only the 2D case (mass and age) was considered, the results represent a lower bound on the difficulty of emulating stellar evolution simulations for precision asteroseismology.

title: Multi-tracer exploration of molecular gas in main sequence galaxies at z~4.5
comment: 12 pages, 1 page Appendix, 6 figures, 2 tables, submitted to A&A
summary: Molecular gas masses in high-z galaxies are inferred from indirect tracers, whose respective reliability remains poorly constrained. In particular, the bright [CII] 158$μ$m line is now widely used as a molecular gas tracer at z>4, yet direct observational tests against CO remain scarce. We search for CO(4-3), CO(5-4), and [CI](1-0) lines in three of the most [CII]-luminous galaxies at z~4.5 from the ALPINE survey to assess the detectability of these lines in high-z main-sequence (MS) galaxies and to test the reliability of [CII] emission as a molecular gas tracer through the cross-comparison of molecular gas masses inferred from six tracers: CO(4-3), CO(5-4), [CI](1-0), [CII], dust continuum, and [CII]-based dynamical mass, adopting standard calibrations and conversion factors. We detect CO(4-3) and CO(5-4) lines at high significance in the near-solar metallicity galaxy DC873756, obtain a tentative CO(4-3) detection in the merging system DC818760, and detect no CO emission in the half-solar metallicity galaxy VC5110377875. [CI] remains undetected in all three galaxies. In DC873756 the molecular gas masses inferred from the six considered tracers agree within their uncertainties despite different systematics inherent to each tracer. The agreement suggests that, at least for some near-solar metallicity MS galaxies at z~4.5, the CO SLED and Milky Way CO-to-H2 conversion factor adopted for MS galaxies at cosmic noon remain applicable and that mid-J CO transitions trace a substantial fraction of the molecular gas reservoir. The CO non-detection in VC5110377875 is consistent with the reduced CO detectability expected at lower metallicities. In DC818760 we find an inconsistency between the [CII]-based molecular gas mass and masses derived from the other tracers, indicating a [CII] excess possibly reflecting enhanced emission from shocks and/or diffuse ionized gas in merger-driven conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper tests the reliability of [CII] 158μm emission as a molecular gas tracer at high redshift by searching for CO(4-3), CO(5-4), and [CI](1-0) lines in three [CII]-luminous galaxies at z~4.5 from the ALPINE survey. They detect CO in two galaxies (near-solar metallicity DC873756 and merging DC818760), but not in the half-solar metallicity galaxy VC5110377875. For the near-solar metallicity galaxy, molecular gas masses inferred from six different tracers agree within uncertainties; however, in the merging system, the [CII]-based mass is inconsistent with other tracers, suggesting a [CII] excess from shocks and/or diffuse ionized gas.
AI.motivation: The [CII] 158μm line is increasingly used to infer molecular gas masses in high-z (z>4) galaxies, but its reliability is poorly constrained because direct observational tests against CO—the canonical tracer—remain scarce. The authors aim to fill this gap by cross-comparing six tracers of molecular gas mass.
AI.method: The authors searched for CO(4-3), CO(5-4), and [CI](1-0) lines in three of the most [CII]-luminous galaxies at z~4.5 from the ALPINE survey using ALMA. They cross-compared molecular gas masses inferred from six tracers—CO(4-3), CO(5-4), [CI](1-0), [CII], dust continuum, and [CII]-based dynamical mass—adopting standard calibrations and conversion factors.
AI.result: CO(4-3) and CO(5-4) were detected at high significance in the near-solar metallicity galaxy DC873756; a tentative CO(4-3) detection was obtained in the merging system DC818760; no CO was detected in the half-solar metallicity galaxy VC5110377875. [CI] remained undetected in all three galaxies. In DC873756, molecular gas masses from all six tracers agreed within uncertainties. In DC818760, the [CII]-based molecular gas mass was inconsistent with other tracers, indicating a [CII] excess possibly from shocks and/or diffuse ionized gas in merger-driven conditions.
AI.conclusion: For at least some near-solar metallicity main-sequence galaxies at z~4.5, the CO SLED and Milky Way CO-to-H2 conversion factor adopted for cosmic noon galaxies remain applicable, and mid-J CO transitions trace a substantial fraction of the molecular gas reservoir. The CO non-detection in VC5110377875 is consistent with reduced CO detectability at lower metallicities. However, [CII] can overestimate molecular gas mass in merger-driven systems due to [CII] excess from shocks/diffuse gas.

title: The scarcity of white dwarf-brown dwarf binaries in the solar neighbourhood: A population synthesis study
comment: 17 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables; accepted for publication in A&A
summary: White dwarf--brown dwarf (WD--BD) binaries are intrinsically rare systems that provide a unique opportunity to study binary evolution and the formation of substellar companions. Despite recent observational progress, only a small number are known in the solar neighbourhood. We investigate whether their scarcity can be explained by binary formation and evolution together with observational selection effects. We extend the MRBIN binary population synthesis code into the substellar regime by incorporating brown dwarf evolutionary models and an extended initial mass function. We simulate the stellar population within 100 pc of the Sun and compare the predicted WD--BD population with the observed sample. Our simulations predict 13+-5 WD--BD systems within 100 pc, consistent with observations. These systems represent only 0.1% of the local white dwarf population, confirming their rarity. The models reproduce the overall distributions of white dwarf masses, temperatures, and orbital periods, although the simulated brown dwarfs are systematically hotter than observed. Close WD--BD binaries are underproduced with the standard common-envelope efficiency 0.3, suggesting that higher efficiencies may be required to reproduce the observed short-period systems. The simulations also reproduce the observed deficit of systems at intermediate orbital periods between post-common-envelope binaries and wide non-interacting systems, as well as a weakened brown dwarf desert in main-sequence--brown dwarf binaries.

AI.tldr: This paper uses the MRBIN binary population synthesis code, extended into the substellar regime, to model white dwarf–brown dwarf binaries within 100 pc of the Sun. The simulations predict 13±5 such systems, consistent with observations, and reproduce observed distributions of WD masses, temperatures, and orbital periods, while highlighting issues with common-envelope efficiency and simulated brown dwarf temperatures.
AI.motivation: White dwarf–brown dwarf binaries are intrinsically rare yet offer unique insights into binary evolution and substellar companion formation. Only a small number are known in the solar neighbourhood, so the authors aim to determine whether this scarcity can be explained by binary formation/evolution physics and observational selection effects.
AI.method: The MRBIN binary population synthesis code is extended into the substellar regime by incorporating brown dwarf evolutionary models and an extended initial mass function. The stellar population within 100 pc of the Sun is simulated and the predicted WD–BD population is compared against the observed sample.
AI.result: Simulations predict 13±5 WD–BD systems within 100 pc, consistent with the observed population and representing only 0.1% of the local white dwarf population. The models reproduce observed distributions of white dwarf masses, temperatures, and orbital periods, though simulated brown dwarfs are systematically hotter than observed. Close WD–BD binaries are underproduced with standard common-envelope efficiency 0.3, suggesting higher efficiencies may be required. The simulations also reproduce deficits at intermediate orbital periods and a weakened brown dwarf desert in main-sequence–brown dwarf binaries.
AI.conclusion: The scarcity of WD–BD binaries in the solar neighbourhood can be explained by binary formation and evolution processes together with observational selection effects. However, higher common-envelope efficiencies than the standard 0.3 may be needed to reproduce short-period systems, and future work is needed to address the temperature discrepancy between simulated and observed brown dwarf companions.

title: CLAS+: A large catalog of Changing-Look AGN candidates selected through S-PLUS narrow-band photometry
comment: Accepted in ApJ. Crossmatch of CLAS+ with LSST is available in https://marixko.github.io/CLAS_lsst_fup/
summary:
Changing-look active galactic nuclei (CLAGN) exhibit rapid spectral transitions on timescales of months to years, challenging standard AGN unification models and providing unique insight into accretion-disk variability and obscuration processes. Despite their scientific importance, systematic searches for CLAGN remain limited by the scarcity of multi-epoch spectroscopy and the difficulty of constructing large samples efficiently.
  We introduce CLAS+, a catalog constructed by comparing synthetic photometry derived from DESI DR1 and SDSS DR17 spectra with contemporaneous narrow-band imaging from the S-PLUS survey.
  Applying our pipeline to a parent sample of 98,139 quasars, we select high-confidence CLAGN candidates above a threshold of reduced chi-squared $χ_r^2 > 15$.
  We identify 3,554 strong CLAGN candidates, corresponding to 3.6\% of the parent sample. This selected fraction is conditional on the adopted criterion and should not be interpreted as an intrinsic CLAGN occurrence rate. Cross-matching with existing CLAGN compilations shows that CLAS+ identifies a large population of previously unreported high-priority candidates (3,481). Among the spectroscopic--photometric comparisons with reliable temporal classification, 40\% are classified as photometric turn-on, 41\% as intermediate, and 19\% as turn-off. We also find an apparent redshift dependence in the relative fractions, with photometric turn-on candidates becoming more common at higher redshifts within the CLAS+ selected sample.
  Therefore, narrow-band photometry provides a powerful and efficient alternative to purely spectroscopic searches for identifying CLAGN candidates at scale. CLAS+ substantially expands the known CLAGN candidate population and provides a valuable target list for future spectroscopic follow-up and time-domain studies with facilities such as Rubin/LSST.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CLAS+, a catalog of changing-look active galactic nuclei (CLAGN) candidates built by comparing synthetic photometry from DESI DR1 and SDSS DR17 spectra with S-PLUS narrow-band imaging. Applying the pipeline to 98,139 quasars, the authors identify 3,554 strong CLAGN candidates (3.6% of the parent sample), including 3,481 previously unreported candidates. Among reliably classified sources, 40% are photometric turn-on, 41% intermediate, and 19% turn-off, with turn-on candidates more common at higher redshifts. The work demonstrates narrow-band photometry as an efficient alternative to purely spectroscopic CLAGN searches and provides a target list for future follow-up.
AI.motivation: CLAGN exhibit rapid spectral transitions that challenge standard AGN unification models, yet systematic searches are limited by the scarcity of multi-epoch spectroscopy and the difficulty of efficiently constructing large samples. The authors aim to overcome these limitations using photometric techniques.
AI.method: The authors construct the CLAS+ catalog by comparing synthetic photometry derived from DESI DR1 and SDSS DR17 spectra with contemporaneous narrow-band imaging from S-PLUS. They apply the pipeline to 98,139 quasars and select high-confidence candidates using a reduced chi-squared threshold of χ²_r > 15.
AI.result: They identify 3,554 strong CLAGN candidates (3.6% of the parent sample), of which 3,481 are previously unreported. Among spectroscopically-photometrically classified candidates, 40% are photometric turn-on, 41% intermediate, and 19% turn-off. A redshift dependence is found, with turn-on candidates more common at higher redshifts.
AI.conclusion: Narrow-band photometry provides a powerful and efficient alternative to purely spectroscopic searches for identifying CLAGN candidates at scale. CLAS+ substantially expands the known CLAGN candidate population and provides a valuable target list for future spectroscopic follow-up and time-domain studies with facilities such as Rubin/LSST.

title: Infrared-excess sources in VVV: candidate debris discs, SED characterization, and variability analysis
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables. Published in MNRAS
summary: Debris disks around main-sequence stars provide important insights into planetary formation and evolution; however, identifying these systems in the Galactic plane, where high interstellar extinction and source crowding are significant, remains challenging. Deep, wide-area surveys such as the VISTA Variables in the Via Lactea (VVV) ESO Public Survey provide multi-epoch infrared observations, enabling systematic searches in these environments. We present a method to construct a refined sample of main-sequence candidates by cross-matching data from Gaia DR3, GLIMPSE, DECaPS, and VIRAC2, to identify infrared excesses through spectral energy distribution (SED) analysis, and to analyse time-series data to detect variability potentially associated with circumstellar material or other astrophysical phenomena. Although infrared excess is commonly associated with debris disks, contributions from unresolved binaries or line-of-sight contamination cannot be excluded. Applying this methodology to the VVV tile d077 using the VIRAC2 catalogue, we analyse an initial sample of 879,556 sources and identify 446 sources flagged by the VO SED Analyser (VOSA) excess-detection algorithm as having infrared excess, of which 171 show candidate periodic variability in the VIRAC2 Ks-band light curves. We further perform SED fitting using theoretical models to derive physical parameters and approximate spectral types for these sources. This work provides a catalogue of infrared-excess candidates in a Galactic field affected by high extinction, along with a reproducible method suitable for future large-scale applications.

AI.tldr: A method is presented to identify main-sequence debris disk candidates in high-extinction Galactic plane fields by cross-matching Gaia DR3, GLIMPSE, DECaPS, and VIRAC2 data, detecting infrared excess via SED analysis, and screening for variability. Applied to VVV tile d077, 446 infrared-excess sources were found from 879,556, of which 171 show periodic variability.
AI.motivation: Debris disks around main-sequence stars are important for understanding planetary formation and evolution, but identifying these systems in the Galactic plane is challenging due to high interstellar extinction and source crowding. This motivates the need for robust methods leveraging deep, multi-epoch infrared surveys like VVV to systematically search for these systems in such environments.
AI.method: The method involves: (1) cross-matching data from Gaia DR3, GLIMPSE, DECaPS, and VIRAC2 to construct a refined sample of main-sequence candidates; (2) identifying infrared excesses through spectral energy distribution (SED) analysis using the VO SED Analyser (VOSA) excess-detection algorithm; (3) analyzing VIRAC2 Ks-band time-series data to detect periodic variability; and (4) performing SED fitting with theoretical models to derive physical parameters and approximate spectral types.
AI.result: Applied to VVV tile d077, an initial sample of 879,556 sources was reduced to 446 sources flagged with infrared excess by VOSA, of which 171 show candidate periodic variability in the Ks-band light curves. Physical parameters and approximate spectral types were derived for these sources via theoretical SED fitting. A catalogue of infrared-excess candidates in this high-extinction Galactic field was produced.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a catalogue of infrared-excess candidates in a heavily extincted Galactic field and establishes a reproducible methodology suitable for future large-scale applications. The authors note that infrared excess may also arise from unresolved binaries or line-of-sight contamination, not solely debris disks, so these candidates require further follow-up for confirmation.

title: Turbulent gas-rich discs at high redshift: the origin of early massive stellar bars
comment: 15 pages, 12 figures. Figs. 4 and 5 reduced in size here for easy comparison. As always, comments welcome
summary: Recent observations combining the power of ALMA and JWST have revealed large ($3-7$ kpc), massive ($3-10\times10^{10}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$) stellar bars at $z=4-5$ when the Universe was only 1.2-1.6 Gyr old. At this early epoch, the host galaxy was baryon-dominated (typically 75\% gas, 25\% stars) within the observed extent of the disc ($8-15$ kpc). Using NEXUS $N$-body/hydrodynamic simulations, we show that such bars can form promptly (400$-$800 Myr), provided the disc mass fraction is high ($f_{\rm disc}\gtrsim 70\%$) and the bar is gas-dominated at the time of its formation, consistent with the observations. In this limit, gas-free bars are unstable to vertical bending modes, but a dominant gas component suppresses this instability. Unlike massive bars in the local Universe, these early bars were sites of vigorous star formation, as we show. Remarkably, for gas-rich models with $f_{\rm gas}\lesssim60\%$, the bars develop X-shaped boxy bulges; at higher gas fractions ($f_{\rm gas}> 60\%$), diffusion suppresses resonant orbit trapping and the emerging bar collapses within 1 Gyr to form a classical bulge. The bar formation time, length, mass, and $m=2$ Fourier amplitude are all inversely related to $f_{\rm gas}$. We present a simple analytic model for how stochastic forcing shifts the bar onset time, defined as the time at which the growing bar amplitude reaches a specified threshold.

AI.tldr: JWST/ALMA observations reveal massive, large stellar bars in high-redshift (z=4-5), gas-dominated galaxies. NEXUS simulations show these bars form promptly when the disc is gas-dominated, with gas suppressing vertical bending instabilities and enabling bar formation. Gas fraction controls bar properties, X-shaped bulges, and eventual fate.
AI.motivation: Recent JWST and ALMA observations have discovered unexpectedly massive and large stellar bars in very early galaxies (z=4-5, only 1.2-1.6 Gyr after Big Bang), in contrast to bars in the local Universe. Understanding how these structures form in gas-dominated, baryon-dominated discs at such early epochs is essential for interpreting these surprising observations.
AI.method: The authors use NEXUS N-body/hydrodynamic simulations to model the formation of bars in high-redshift gas-rich discs, varying the gas fraction and disc mass fraction to explore the parameter space consistent with observations.
AI.result: Bars can form promptly (400-800 Myr) only when the disc mass fraction is high (f_disc > 70%) and the bar is gas-dominated at formation. Gas suppresses vertical bending instability that destroys gas-free bars. For gas fractions < 60%, X-shaped boxy bulges develop; for > 60%, the bar collapses within 1 Gyr to form a classical bulge. Bar formation time, length, mass, and m=2 amplitude all inversely scale with gas fraction. A simple analytic model for stochastic forcing shifting bar onset time is presented.
AI.conclusion: Early bars in gas-dominated discs are viable and had vigorous star formation, unlike local bars. The gas fraction is a key parameter governing bar properties and long-term evolution, linking early bar formation to distinct bulge morphologies.

title: Bifurcations in the Heliosphere: Global-scale Coronal Pseudostreamer Evolution and the Creation of Secondary Heliospheric Current Sheets
comment: 16 pages 8 figures Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The heliospheric current sheet (HCS) is the boundary between open magnetic fields of opposite polarity in the solar wind that connect back to their respective open flux regions in the corona. The HCS is often described as a disc-like sheet warped by the combined effects of the inclination of the magnetic equator on the Sun, solar rotation, and solar wind expansion. The HCS is an extension of the helmet streamer belt-the closed-flux region resulting from the global dipole component of the observed photospheric magnetic field. In the absence of a strong dipole, a dominant quadrupole can result in two separate HCSs. Here we report on a set of idealized, axisymmetric solar wind simulations designed to study the transition of the single-HCS corona and inner heliosphere into a multiple-HCS configuration, run with the WindPredict-AW PLUTO MHD code. We systematically vary the relative strengths of the dipole/quadrupole contributions to the global field and show this results in the formation of a large-scale, closed-flux pseudostreamer that interacts with the ambient solar wind. We find that when the dipole and quadrupole magnitudes are approximately equal, our model corona can oscillate between a one- and two-HCS configuration on the timescale of days-to-weeks. We characterize the plasma dynamics of the transition of a global-scale pseudostreamer into a localized, secondary helmet-streamer belt with its own HCS surrounding a newly-opened, opposite-polarity coronal hole. We discuss the implications of our results for solar cycle evolution and the dynamic coupling of the highly structured corona and inner heliosphere.

AI.tldr: This paper uses idealized, axisymmetric solar wind MHD simulations (WindPredict-AW PLUTO code) to study how the heliospheric current sheet (HCS) transitions from a single to a multiple configuration as the relative strengths of the solar dipole and quadrupole magnetic field components vary. When these components are nearly equal, the model corona oscillates between one- and two-HCS states on timescales of days to weeks, involving transient pseudostreamer formation and secondary helmet-streamer belts with newly opened opposite-polarity coronal holes.
AI.motivation: Understanding how the heliospheric current sheet transitions from a single-HCS configuration (dominated by the solar dipole) into a multiple-HCS configuration (dominated by higher-order multipoles such as a quadrupole) is crucial for understanding solar cycle evolution and the dynamic coupling between the structured corona and inner heliosphere.
AI.method: Idealized, axisymmetric solar wind simulations are run using the WindPredict-AW PLUTO MHD code. The relative strengths of the dipole and quadrupole contributions to the global photospheric magnetic field are systematically varied to study how this controls the morphology of the HCS and the formation of large-scale closed-flux pseudostreamers interacting with the ambient solar wind.
AI.result: When dipole and quadrupole magnitudes are approximately equal, the model corona can oscillate between one- and two-HCS configurations on a timescale of days to weeks. The simulations capture the plasma dynamics of a global-scale pseudostreamer transitioning into a localized, secondary helmet-streamer belt with its own HCS surrounding a newly-opened, opposite-polarity coronal hole.
AI.conclusion: The simulations reveal that transitions between single- and multiple-HCS configurations are dynamically rich and occur when the dominant multipoles of the global field are of comparable strength. These results have implications for understanding solar cycle evolution and the dynamic coupling of the highly structured corona and inner heliosphere.

title: Evolution of Virial Clouds - II: From the Formation of First Stars up to their Explosion
comment: 14 pages, 8 figures
summary: The existence of cold gas and dust clouds close to the cosmic microwave background (CMB) temperature was proposed as a potential repository for a significant fraction of the missing baryons in galactic halos. While the evolution of the virial clouds from the last scattering surface (LSS) ($z=1100$) up to the formation of Population III (Pop III) stars ($z=48$) was studied in [N. Tahir, A. Qadir, M. Sakhi, \& F. De Paolis, The Euro. Phys. Jour. C 81, 827 (2021)] (Paper I), the subsequent evolution during the epoch of the first stars remained unexplored. In the present work, we investigate the second evolutionary phase of the virial clouds, covering the redshift range $48 \gtrsim z \gtrsim 10$. We develop a comprehensive model incorporating the coupled thermal, chemical, and dynamical evolution of the cloud, including CMB heating, adiabatic compression due to gravitational contraction, H$_2$ and metal-line cooling, and feedback from Pop III supernovae. Solving the coupled ordinary differential equations (ODE) numerically, we find that the cloud cools monotonically from $137$~K to $41.5$~K, contracts from $120$~pc to $89.8$~pc, and becomes enriched in metals and molecular hydrogen, while the cooling rate dominates the heating rate throughout the evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the second evolutionary phase of cold virial gas clouds in galactic halos during the epoch of first stars (redshift 48 to 10), modeling their coupled thermal, chemical, and dynamical evolution. The cloud cools from 137 K to 41.5 K, contracts from 120 pc to 89.8 pc, and becomes enriched in metals and molecular hydrogen, with cooling dominating heating throughout.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to extend the earlier work (Paper I) that studied virial cloud evolution from the last scattering surface (z=1100) to Pop III star formation (z=48). The subsequent evolution during the epoch of first stars (z=48 to z=10) was previously unexplored, leaving a gap in understanding whether such clouds could serve as repositories for missing baryons in galactic halos.
AI.method: A comprehensive model is developed incorporating coupled thermal, chemical, and dynamical evolution of the virial cloud. The model includes CMB heating, adiabatic compression from gravitational contraction, H2 and metal-line cooling, and feedback from Pop III supernovae. The coupled ordinary differential equations (ODEs) are solved numerically over the redshift range 48 to 10.
AI.result: The numerical solutions show the cloud cools monotonically from 137 K to 41.5 K and contracts from 120 pc to 89.8 pc over the explored redshift range. The cloud becomes enriched in metals and molecular hydrogen throughout its evolution, with the cooling rate dominating the heating rate at all times.
AI.conclusion: The virial clouds continue to cool and contract during the epoch of first stars, remaining viable as cold gas and dust reservoirs potentially harboring a significant fraction of missing baryons in galactic halos through this later evolutionary phase.

title: NGC 1901: A new benchmark cluster for gyrochronology in the TESS Southern continuous viewing zone
comment: Submitted to MNRAS
summary: We use Gaia DR3 astrometry and TESS time-series photometry to study NGC 1901, a sparse open cluster in the TESS Southern continuous viewing zone, that has been neglected due to its proximity on the sky to the Large Magellanic Cloud. We refine its membership list and measure rotation periods for 32 high-confidence rotating stars. By applying the gyro-interp empirical model, we calculate a gyrochronal age of 830 $\pm$ 50 Myr. Because NGC 1901 possesses a sub-solar metallicity of [Fe/H]$\approx -0.11$, its excellent agreement with empirical models suggests that temperature-period relations mitigate metallicity effects for Sun-like stars. Our results place NGC 1901 in the gap between the benchmark open clusters Praesepe (670 Myr) and NGC 6811 (1 Gyr). We find that the rotation sequence exhibits significant spin-down stalling in late K dwarfs, supporting models of core--envelope recoupling. Furthermore, our findings provide constraints for the cluster's structural evolution, including its recently identified tidal tail and corona. This study establishes NGC 1901 as a new benchmark for calibrating the next generation of gyrochronal models.

The rotation sequence shows spin-down stalling in late K dwarfs, supporting core–envelope recoupling models, and providing constraints on the cluster's structural evolution including its tidal tail and corona.

AI.method: Combines Gaia DR3 astrometry for membership refinement with TESS time-series photometry to measure rotation periods for 32 high-confidence rotating stars. Applies the gyro-interp empirical model to compute a gyrochronal age. Evaluates the cluster's sub-solar metallicity against empirical temperature-period relations and analyzes the rotation sequence for spin-down behavior in late K dwarfs.

title: Search for intranight optical variability in a large sample of intermediate-mass black holes
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: Using the extensive archival database of the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) survey, we have investigated intranight optical variability (INOV) in a large sample of low-mass active galactic nuclei (LMAGN) powered by intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs). After applying a sequence of well-motivated selection filters, we constructed an unbiased, representative sample of 62 IMBHs for which $r$-band intranight photometric sequences are available in the ZTF database, yielding 167 sessions with a minimum duration of 2 h. By performing aperture photometry on the sequence of exposures in each session, we derived differential light curves (DLCs) of the target LMAGN relative to two carefully selected non-varying comparison stars monitored simultaneously with the LMAGN in the same exposure sequence. Application of the widely used test based on $F$-statistics to all these DLCs revealed no case of statistically significant INOV. We discuss this result for the present large sample of LMAGN in the context of an earlier report of INOV detections in another, albeit much smaller and differently selected, sample of LMAGN that had been monitored in targeted observations.

AI.tldr: Using ZTF archival data, the authors constructed a representative sample of 62 low-mass AGNs powered by intermediate-mass black holes and monitored them across 167 intranight sessions. No statistically significant intranight optical variability was detected, contrasting with earlier claims from smaller targeted samples.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether low-mass AGNs powered by intermediate-mass black holes exhibit intranight optical variability (INOV), especially given conflicting earlier reports from small targeted samples. A large, unbiased sample is needed to settle this question statistically.
AI.method: Selection of 62 IMBH-powered LMAGN from ZTF archival data via well-motivated filters; acquisition of 167 r-band intranight photometric sessions (≥2h each); aperture photometry to derive differential light curves relative to two non-varying comparison stars; application of F-statistics tests to assess variability.
AI.result: No statistically significant INOV was detected in any of the 167 sessions across the 62-object sample, despite the large, unbiased sample size and adequate monitoring durations.
AI.conclusion: The absence of INOV in this large sample of LMAGN contrasts with earlier positive detections in a smaller, differently selected targeted sample, suggesting that reported INOV in such sources may depend on sample selection or may not be a common/persistent property of these objects.

title: The Role of Preceding CMEs and SIRs in Enhancing Shock Acceleration of Electrons
summary: The role of large-scale pre-existing interplanetary structures, including preceding coronal mass ejections (CMEs) and stream interaction regions (SIRs), in shaping the shock acceleration environment for energetic electrons remains not fully understood. In this study, we investigate nine interplanetary shocks observed by the Solar Terrestrial Relations Observatory (STEREO) that are associated with significant MeV electron enhancements, as such enhancements are rarely observed at interplanetary shocks. We combine remote-sensing observations, drag-based modeling, and in-situ measurements to analyze the shock propagation through pre-existing interplanetary structures. Eight of the nine events are associated with a preceding slow or intermediate-speed CME, while six shocks are in-situ observed propagating within preceding ICMEs, indicating that large-scale upstream trapping structures are a common feature of these events. Further analysis identifies three distinct scenarios associated with enhanced electron acceleration: shocks propagating through preceding ICMEs, shock-SIR interactions, and direct injection of flare-accelerated electrons into SIRs. As a representative shock-in-ICME event, the 2012 January 29 low-$β$, quasi-perpendicular shock ($θ_{Bn}\sim87^\circ$) is further investigated using observations together with one-dimensional Monte Carlo test-particle simulations of a shock propagating into a large-scale upstream magnetic loop. The simulation suggests that the upstream loop prolongs electron residence near the shock and substantially enhances acceleration efficiency. These results demonstrate that large-scale interplanetary structures can precondition the upstream magnetic environment, providing favorable conditions for prolonged electron residence and efficient shock acceleration.

AI.tldr: The study investigates nine interplanetary shocks observed by STEREO that produced significant MeV electron enhancements, finding that most were preceded by CMEs or SIRs. Three distinct acceleration scenarios are identified: shock propagation through preceding ICMEs, shock-SIR interactions, and direct injection of flare-accelerated electrons into SIRs. Using the 2012 January 29 event and Monte Carlo simulations, the authors demonstrate that large-scale upstream magnetic structures (e.g., ICMEs, magnetic loops) can precondition the upstream environment, prolonging electron residence near the shock and enhancing acceleration efficiency.
AI.motivation: Significant MeV electron enhancements at interplanetary shocks are rarely observed, and the role of large-scale pre-existing interplanetary structures (preceding CMEs and SIRs) in shaping the shock acceleration environment for energetic electrons remains not fully understood.
AI.method: Nine STEREO-observed interplanetary shocks associated with significant MeV electron enhancements are analyzed by combining remote-sensing observations, drag-based modeling, and in-situ measurements. A representative shock-in-ICME event (2012 January 29, low-β, quasi-perpendicular shock with θ_Bn ~87°) is further investigated using 1D Monte Carlo test-particle simulations of a shock propagating into an upstream magnetic loop.
AI.result: Eight of nine events were associated with a preceding slow or intermediate-speed CME, and six shocks propagated within preceding ICMEs. Three distinct acceleration scenarios were identified: shocks propagating through preceding ICMEs, shock-SIR interactions, and direct injection of flare-accelerated electrons into SIRs. Simulations show that the upstream magnetic loop prolongs electron residence and substantially enhances shock acceleration efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale interplanetary structures precondition the upstream magnetic environment, creating favorable conditions for prolonged electron residence and efficient shock acceleration of MeV electrons.

title: Constraints on mu-variations from the methanol CH3OH thermal lines in the Galaxy at galactocentric distances of 1.5 < D_GC < 13 kpc
comment: 19 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables; accepted for publication in JETP Letters
summary: In this study, constraints are set on hypothetical variations of the fundamental physical constant mu = m_e/m_p - the electron-to-proton mass ratio - based on thermal emission lines of E-methanol (CH3OH) in the 216-220 GHz frequency range. Molecular spectra toward seven massive clouds located across a wide range of galactocentric distances (1.5 < D_GC < 13 kpc) have been analyzed. The obtained weighted mean value <Delta mu/mu> = (0.5+/-0.5)*10^(-7) does not indicate statistically significant changes in mu at the 1 sigma confidence level of 5*10^(-8), which is in good agreement with previously established upper limits in a number of molecular clouds in the Galactic disk.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes E-methanol thermal emission lines in the 216-220 GHz range toward seven massive molecular clouds across the Galactic disk to constrain variations in the electron-to-proton mass ratio (mu = m_e/m_p). The weighted mean value <Delta mu/mu> = (0.5±0.5)×10⁻⁷ shows no statistically significant change in mu at the 1σ level (5×10⁻⁸), consistent with earlier upper limits.
AI.motivation: To test fundamental physics hypotheses regarding possible spatial or temporal variations of the electron-to-proton mass ratio (mu) across the Galaxy by using high-precision molecular spectroscopy toward clouds at different galactocentric distances.
AI.method: Observational spectroscopy of E-methanol (CH3OH) thermal emission lines in the 216-220 GHz frequency range toward seven massive clouds spanning galactocentric distances from 1.5 to 13 kpc, followed by a weighted mean analysis of Delta mu/mu.
AI.result: The derived weighted mean <Delta mu/mu> = (0.5±0.5)×10⁻⁷ indicates no statistically significant variation in mu at the 1σ confidence level of 5×10⁻⁸, consistent with previously established upper limits in Galactic disk molecular clouds.
AI.conclusion: The results support the constancy of the electron-to-proton mass ratio in the Galactic disk within the achieved sensitivity, confirming earlier upper-limit measurements.

title: New scaling relations from MESA models for mass and radius of subgiant stars: application to Kepler targets
comment: 15 pages, 13 figures
summary: The precise determination of the fundamental parameters of stars is crucial for understanding stellar structure and evolution. In this regard, the asteroseismic parameters of solar-like oscillating stars obtained from space telescopes are very useful for determining the mass ($M$) and radius ($R$) of single stars using classical scaling relations. These relations still need to be improved. In this study, we develop alternative scaling relations based on reference frequencies ($ν_{\rm min}$) due to helium ionization zone glitches, specifically for subgiant (SG) stars. We compile main-sequence and SG {\small{MESA}} models from the literature and derive new scaling relations for stellar $R$ and surface gravity ($g$) of evolved stars. The expressions for $R$ and $g$ are obtained simultaneously as functions of the large frequency separation, $ν_{\rm min}$, and metallicity. These new relations allow $M$ and $R$ to be reliably determined only from observational parameters, without the need for detailed stellar modelling. The resulting $ν_{\rm min}$-based relations are applied to a sample of 31 SG stars observed by the \emph{Kepler} mission, with masses in the range 0.85-1.74 M$_\odot$ and radii between 1.03 and 2.82 R$_\odot$. Using simultaneous solutions, we estimate new mass and radius ranges of 0.89-1.62 M$_\odot$ and 1.04-2.95 R$_\odot$, respectively. The results demonstrate significant improvements in the determination of $M$ and $R$ for evolved \emph{Kepler} target stars, highlighting the potential of the new scaling relations in asteroseismic analyses.

AI.tldr: The paper develops alternative asteroseismic scaling relations based on reference frequencies (ν_min) from helium ionization zone glitches to determine mass and radius of subgiant stars, circumventing classical scaling relation limitations. Applied to 31 Kepler subgiant stars, the new relations yield improved mass estimates (0.89-1.62 M⊙) and radii (1.04-2.95 R⊙) without requiring detailed stellar modeling.
AI.motivation: Precise determination of stellar fundamental parameters (M, R) is essential for understanding stellar structure and evolution. Classical asteroseismic scaling relations for solar-like oscillators still require improvement, particularly for evolved (subgiant) stars. The authors aim to develop more reliable scaling relations using ν_min (from helium ionization zone glitches) to avoid the need for detailed stellar modeling.
AI.method: Compile main-sequence and subgiant MESA stellar models from the literature. Derive new scaling relations for stellar radius (R) and surface gravity (g) as simultaneous functions of the large frequency separation, ν_min, and metallicity. These relations express R and g analytically, enabling M and R inference purely from observed asteroseismic and spectroscopic parameters.
AI.result: Applying the ν_min-based scaling relations to 31 Kepler-observed subgiant stars (0.85-1.74 M⊙, 1.03-2.82 R⊙), simultaneous solutions yield revised mass and radius ranges of 0.89-1.62 M⊙ and 1.04-2.95 R⊙, respectively, demonstrating significant improvements over classical relations for evolved stars.
AI.conclusion: The new ν_min-based scaling relations improve the determination of mass and radius for evolved Kepler targets and highlight the potential of helium-ionization-glitch-based reference frequencies in future asteroseismic analyses, reducing reliance on detailed stellar modeling.

title: Magnetic Fields in Massive Star-forming Regions (MagMaR). XII. Radiative Torque Alignment and Disruption in NGC6334I
comment: 35 pages, 29 figures, and 3 tables
summary: Intense radiation from high-mass stars is expected to significantly affect dust grain alignment and evolution through RAdiative Torques (RATs). We investigate this effect in a massive star-forming region, NGC6334I, using 1.2 mm dust continuum polarization observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. The polarization fraction spans from $\lesssim1\%$ to $\sim10\%$ and decreases with increasing column density, remaining below $2\%$ in dense cores despite high temperatures ($\sim100$ K), where efficient grain alignment by RATs is expected. We investigate how grain alignment, grain growth, grain disruption, B-field tangling, and local physical conditions affect the polarization properties of MM1, MM2, MM3, and their surroundings. Polarization angle dispersion shows that B-field tangling contributes to depolarization at moderate densities but cannot fully explain the lowest polarization fractions. Using RAT-based grain alignment and polarization modeling, we find that reduced alignment efficiency and high optical depth reproduce the low polarization in the densest regions. MM2 shows evidence of grain growth, with maximum grain sizes $a_{\max}\sim0.35-1.0~μ$m, while MM1 exhibits smaller values of $\sim0.35-0.50~μ$m. Accounting for optical depth increases the inferred grain sizes in MM1 to $\sim1.0-2.0~μ$m. Analytical estimates of radiative torque disruption from the intense outburst suggest that micron-sized grains in high-temperature, moderate-density regions can fragment into submicron grains. Alternatively, high optical depth may also explain the low polarization in the densest regions even in the presence of micron-sized grains. Incorporating the B-field inclination effect indicates a transition from predominantly plane-of-sky fields at low densities to more line-of-sight-aligned configurations at high densities.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates dust grain alignment and evolution in the massive star-forming region NGC6334I using ALMA 1.2 mm dust continuum polarization observations. The polarization fraction ranges from <1% to ~10% and decreases with column density, remaining below 2% in dense cores despite high temperatures (~100 K). The authors find that reduced alignment efficiency, high optical depth, and B-field tangling collectively explain the low polarization, and identify grain growth up to ~1-2 μm in the dense cores, with radiative torque disruption potentially fragmenting micron-sized grains in high-temperature, moderate-density regions.
AI.motivation: To understand how intense radiation from high-mass stars affects dust grain alignment and evolution in massive star-forming regions through RAdiative Torques (RATs), which has implications for interpreting polarized dust emission as a tracer of magnetic fields and grain properties.
AI.method: The study uses ALMA 1.2 mm dust continuum polarization observations of NGC6334I and its subregions MM1, MM2, MM3. It analyzes polarization fraction, polarization angle dispersion (for B-field tangling), applies RAT-based grain alignment and polarization modeling, computes analytical estimates of radiative torque disruption, and accounts for optical depth and B-field inclination effects.
AI.result: Polarization fraction spans <1% to ~10%, decreasing with column density and staying below 2% in dense cores despite ~100 K temperatures. B-field tangling contributes to depolarization at moderate densities but cannot fully explain the lowest fractions. Reduced alignment efficiency and high optical depth reproduce the low polarization in the densest regions. MM2 shows grain growth with max grain sizes ~0.35-1.0 μm, MM1 ~0.35-0.50 μm (increasing to ~1.0-2.0 μm when optical depth is considered). Radiative torque disruption can fragment micron-sized grains into submicron grains in high-temperature, moderate-density regions. B-field inclination transitions from predominantly plane-of-sky at low densities to line-of-sight-aligned at high densities.
AI.conclusion: The low polarization in dense cores of NGC6334I arises from a combination of reduced RAT alignment efficiency, high optical depth, and B-field tangling, rather than solely from temperature effects. Grain growth has occurred in these regions, but radiative torque disruption from the outburst may hinder growth of micron-sized grains in some environments. High optical depth can alternatively explain low polarization even with micron-sized grains present, and the magnetic field geometry transitions from plane-of-sky to line-of-sight dominated with increasing density.

title: Interferometric Survey of Stellar Parameters: Mass of the metallic A-type binary $β$ Aur
comment: 17 pages, 9 figures, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: With the capabilities of the new visible CHARA/SPICA instrument and the multiple spectral band operation of CHARA, our goal is to resolve orbits of short-period binaries and develop a robust framework for combining interferometric, spectroscopic, and photometric observations into a single consistent model. For our target sample, we selected suitable binaries based on brightness, angular separation, and orbital properties based on the expected performance of the CHARA/SPICA instrument. As a case study, we analysed the bright eclipsing binary $β$ Aurigae, composed of two slightly evolved A1 stars. We combined new interferometric observations of $β$ Aur obtained with CHARA/SPICA, MIRC-X, and MYSTIC with archival MIRC data, radial velocities, and light curves. We first derived astrometric positions from interferometric observables and computed an orbital solution. Afterwards, we implemented a unified model, capable of tying interferometric modelling with the ellc code to simultaneously fit all observables using MCMC sampling. We performed a detailed analysis of the noise statistics of each data set and in the end we adopted a profile likelihood approach to account for underestimated noise and systematics. We derived a consistent orbital and physical solution for $β$ Aur through joint modelling. The inclusion of interferometric data tightly constrains the angular semi-major axis and inclination. Using profile likelihood to account for the different intrinsic levels of uncertainty of the fundamentally different observables, we derived the masses of the two stars, $M_1 = 2.359 \pm 0.005$ M$_S$ and $M_2 = 2.293 \pm 0.004$ M$_S$, their radii $R_1 = 2.752 \pm 0.002$ R$_S$ and $R_2 = 2.622 \pm 0.002$ R$_S$, and the distance to the binary, $d = 24.30\pm0.05$ pc.

The joint modeling yields precise masses (M1=2.359±0.005 M☉, M2=2.293±0.004 M☉), radii (R1=2.752±0.002 R☉, R2=2.622±0.002 R☉), and distance (d=24.30±0.05 pc).

For the case-study binary β Aurigae, new interferometric observations from CHARA/SPICA, MIRC-X, and MYSTIC were combined with archival MIRC data, radial velocities, and light curves. Astrometric positions were derived from interferometric observables and used to compute an orbital solution. A unified model was then implemented linking interferometric modeling with the ellc code to fit all observables simultaneously via MCMC sampling, with a detailed noise-statistics analysis and a profile-likelihood approach adopted to account for underestimated noise and systematics.

title: Bright star-forming galaxies naturally forming at z>10 in the Shark semi-analytic model
comment: 20 pages, 9 figures. Submitted to MNRAS. Comments welcome!
summary: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has unveiled the existence of numerous z>10 bright ultraviolet (UV) galaxies, potentially challenging galaxy formation models in a Lambda Cold Dark Matter (LCDM) universe. Modifications to star formation and stellar feedback models have been suggested to alleviate the tension. However, the fundamental challenge is to design a galaxy formation model that simultaneously reproduces observations from z=0 to those at the highest redshifts. Here, we present predictions from the Shark semi-analytic model of galaxy formation, which is tuned to reproduce the z=0 universe. We show that the same model is capable of reproducing the current UV luminosity function constraints even up to z=17 without the need to invoke variations in the baryon physics model. This model is also capable of reproducing reasonably well the stellar mass function evolution from z=0 to z=10 and the cosmic star formation rate (SFR) density at 0<z<15, again with the same baryon physics and parameters. The key to the success of Shark is the triggering of starbursts by violent disk instabilities included in the model, which leads to an increase in the variance of the UV luminosity with increasing halo mass at z>10. We demonstrate that without this mechanism, galaxies are not bursty enough in the model to reproduce the observations at z>10.

AI.tldr: The Shark semi-analytic galaxy formation model, tuned to reproduce z=0 observations, successfully reproduces JWST-detected UV luminosity functions up to z=17 and other high-redshift constraints without modifying baryon physics. The key mechanism enabling this is starbursts triggered by violent disk instabilities, which increase UV luminosity variance in high-mass halos at z>10.
AI.motivation: JWST has discovered numerous bright UV galaxies at z>10 that may challenge standard galaxy formation models in a LCDM universe. While modifications to star formation and stellar feedback have been proposed, the fundamental challenge is developing a single model that simultaneously reproduces observations from z=0 to the highest redshifts.
AI.method: The authors use the Shark semi-analytic model of galaxy formation, which is tuned to match z=0 observations. They test whether this same model, without any variations in baryon physics or parameters, can reproduce high-redshift UV luminosity functions and related observables. They specifically examine the role of violent disk instabilities triggering starbursts in producing bursty star formation at high redshifts.

title: Ionized Nebulae Around Two New Symbiotic Stars: GR Cygni and [D75] 141
comment: Accepted by PASP
summary: In the course of selecting targets for a spectroscopic survey of faint planetary-nebula nuclei, we encountered two anomalous cases of late-type variable stars surrounded by nebulosities discovered by amateur astronomers. Both central stars, respectively GR Cygni and [D75] 141, are found to be pulsating semiregular variable stars. Our spectroscopic observations show GR Cyg to be a cool carbon star of type C9,2, with emission lines of the Balmer series, [O II] and [O III], [Ne III], [S II], and Fe II. A synthetic narrow-band image of GR Cyg shows that the source of its strong [O II] 3727 A emission line is a knot displaced from the star by about 1.6 arcsec, indicative of a recent collimated ejection event. title: C3PO: A Lyα Emitting Galaxy at $z \sim 9$
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures, comments are welcome
summary: We present deep, $>10$ hr, JWST NIRSpec G140M and G395M observations of a previously known galaxy C3PO-8447 at $z=8.99781$. Our new NIRSpec data from the Carbon-3 plus Oxygen (C3PO) survey detect Ly$α$ emission with an escape fraction of $1.5\pm0.3\%$ and a velocity offset of $210\pm80$ km s$^{-1}$, making C3PO-8447 the third Ly$α$ emitting galaxy confirmed at $z\gtrsim 9$. The galaxy has a low stellar mass of $2.2\pm0.1\times 10^7\ M_\odot$, a young stellar age of $1.6\pm0.2$ Myr, and a low oxygen abundance of $12+\log(\mathrm{O/H}) = 7.50\pm0.08$. UV diagnostic diagrams incorporating the C IV, O III], and C III] emission lines indicate that the ionization of C3PO-8447 is dominated by the recent starburst. The low Ly$α$ escape fraction of C3PO-8447 implies that C3PO-8447 resides in a small ionized bubble with radius $R \sim 0.07$ to 0.20 pMpc, which can be produced by C3PO-8447 alone. We find no evidence for either a large-scale galaxy overdensity around C3PO-8447 or a significant contribution from nearby galaxies to its ionizing photon budget. Taken together, these results suggest that C3PO-8447 likely represents an ionized bubble powered by a single low-mass, vigorously star-forming galaxy during the early stages of cosmic reionization.

title: Rapid Growth of Intermediate-Mass Black Holes through Disk-induced Stellar DisruptionsRapid Growth of Intermediate-Mass Black Holes through Disk-induced Stellar Disruptions
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to ApJ
summary: Dense nuclear star clusters provide unique environments for studying the dynamical interactions between stars and massive black holes. When an accretion disk is present, dissipative star--disk interactions can capture surrounding stars, drive their inward migration, and ultimately lead to disk-induced tidal disruption events\,(dTDEs). The long-term feeding rate from this process, however, cannot be inferred from single-orbit migration estimates alone, as it depends on the coupled evolution of disk capture, collisional relaxation, stellar depletion and replenishment, and physical mergers within the star cluster. In this work, we use high-performance direct $N$-body simulations combined with analytic prescriptions for star--disk interactions to follow this coupled evolution for intermediate-mass black holes\,(IMBHs) with accretion disks embedded in dense stellar clusters. The simulations track the formation of the stellar cusp, the capture of stars by repeated disk crossings, their subsequent orbital damping and migration, and their eventual consumption by the central IMBH. We find that dTDEs can sustain stellar mass supply rates of $\sim10^{-3}\,M_\odot \,\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, which exceeds the Eddington-limited gas accretion rate for IMBHs with $M_\bullet<10^5\,M_\odot$. These results identify dTDEs as an efficient stellar feeding channel for IMBHs in gas-rich dense stellar systems. As one possible application, this mechanism may help transform $\sim10^3\,M_\odot$ IMBHs into more massive black-hole seeds, provided that compact stellar clusters and accretion disks persist for $>30$ Myr.

title: Two sets of potential-density basis pairs for the study of radial perturbations in collisionless spherical stellar systems
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures. Accepted for publication in MNRAS
summary: The Kalnajs matrix method is a widely used framework for studying the global linear stability and possible Landau damping of collisionless stellar systems. However, for radial perturbations ($l=0$) in three-dimensional spherical models with infinite boundaries, standard biorthogonal sets such as the Clutton-Brock basis often converge slowly. This stems from a physical constraint: mass-conserving radial modes force the perturbed potential to decay faster than a point mass at infinity, whereas individual Clutton-Brock elements carry a fictitious net mass and decay only as $\mathcal{O}(1/r)$, producing unphysical asymptotic tails. We construct two new families of potential-density basis pairs that are free of these tails by construction. The first modifies the Clutton-Brock set: a specific linear combination of adjacent elements analytically cancels the leading $\mathcal{O}(1/r)$ term, giving potentials that decay as $\mathcal{O}(1/r^3)$ and densities as $\mathcal{O}(1/r^5)$. This breaks strict biorthogonality but yields a compact tridiagonal Gram matrix that enters the response equation at negligible additional cost. The second family is built from Jacobi polynomials that embed the required $\mathcal{O}(1/r^2)$ potential decay directly into their construction while retaining strict diagonal biorthogonality. Numerical tests demonstrate convergence that is uniform in radius for both expansions: the truncation error decreases exponentially when the asymptotic tail of the expanded potential matches the parity of the basis elements, and algebraically otherwise. Both bases reduce the dimension of the response matrix required for a given accuracy and are suited to studying radial perturbations in open stellar systems.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the slow convergence of the Kalnajs matrix method for radial (l=0) perturbations in open spherical stellar systems, caused by fictitious net mass in standard Clutton-Brock basis elements producing unphysical asymptotic tails. Two new basis families are constructed that eliminate these tails: one via linear combinations of Clutton-Brock elements (yielding a tridiagonal Gram matrix), and another from Jacobi polynomials with embedded O(1/r²) potential decay. Both achieve uniform exponential convergence in radius when parity matches, improving the efficiency of response-matrix computations.
AI.motivation: The Kalnajs matrix method suffers from slow convergence for radial perturbations in 3D spherical models because mass-conserving modes require potential decay faster than 1/r, while standard Clutton-Brock basis elements carry fictitious net mass decaying as O(1/r), producing unphysical asymptotic tails that slow convergence.
